cards.front: Which component must exist for an operating system to execute Java bytecode?
cards.extra: javac compiles to bytecode aimed at the JVM instruction set, not at a CPU. Each OS/architecture needs its own JVM build to execute that bytecode, which is why the installer is OS-specific even though your .class files are not.
cards.example:
java Hello      # runs on any OS that has a JVM for it
javac Hello.java  # the compiler ships with the JDK

cards.front: Which single installation gives you javac, the JVM and the standard library?
cards.extra: The JDK bundles the compiler javac, the launcher java, the standard library and tools such as jar and javadoc. Since JDK 11 no separate JRE is published, so 'install the JRE' is no longer the way you set up a machine.
cards.example:
javac -version   # compiler
java -version    # JVM + standard library, all from one JDK install

cards.question: Name the three layers, outermost first.
cards.extra: Read the nesting outward-in: the JDK contains the JRE, which contains the JVM. A developer installs the JDK; a production container can ship a smaller runtime built with jlink.
cards.example:
javac Hello.java   # JDK: compiler
java Hello         # JRE/JVM: runtime

cards.front: What does the JVM do that makes "write once, run anywhere" true?
cards.back: It executes the same portable bytecode on every platform
cards.extra: Compiling to bytecode means the same .class file runs on Linux, Windows and macOS. Only the JVM is platform-specific; the compiled artifact is not.
cards.example:
javac Hello.java   # compile once
java Hello         # every JVM runs the same bytecode

cards.question: Which region holds the object, and which holds the reference to it?
cards.extra: Each thread gets its own stack of frames, and a frame holds primitives plus references. Objects and arrays live on the shared heap, and the reference on the stack points at one.
cards.example:
class Person { String name; }
class Demo {
    void run() {
        Person p = new Person();   // the object sits on the heap
                                   // p, the reference, is a local in this frame
    }
}

cards.front: When you assign one object variable to another, what is copied?
cards.extra: Person b = a; copies the pointer, not the object. Both names now target the same instance, so a change through one is visible through the other.
cards.example:
int[] a = {1, 2};
int[] b = a;      // the reference is copied
b[0] = 9;
System.out.println(a[0]);   // 9 - one array, two references

cards.text: An object becomes eligible for garbage collection when {{c1::no live reference reaches it}}.
cards.extra: Eligibility is about reachability: the collector follows references from GC roots (stack frames, static fields). Once no path reaches the object it may be reclaimed, and nothing tells you exactly when.
cards.example:
Object o = new Object();
o = null;          // nothing reachable: now eligible for collection

cards.front: Which memory area is per thread, and which is shared?
cards.back: Stack per thread; heap shared by all threads
cards.extra: Stacks are private, so a local variable is invisible to other threads; the heap is shared, so two threads can touch the same object. Data races live in that overlap.
cards.example:
Runnable task = () -> { int local = 1; };   // locals live on that thread's stack
new Thread(task).start();                     // objects go to the shared heap

cards.question: Collections and Concurrency sit in the same band. Which one?
cards.back: 02 Data and flow — the band above the language core
cards.extra: Band 02 sits on the language core: collections, lambdas and threads all manipulate objects, so they only make sense once classes, references and interfaces are clear. Band 01 is pure language; band 04 is engineering practice.
cards.example: // 02 Data and flow: collections and concurrency sit above the language core

cards.front: Why does the roadmap put Collections after the object model?
cards.back: Collections store and compare object references, relying on equals / hashCode
cards.extra: HashSet and HashMap decide where an entry goes with hashCode and whether two entries are the same with equals — both inherited methods you can override. That is why the object model comes first.
cards.example: Set seen = new HashSet<>();   // dedup relies on equals and hashCode

cards.front: Which roadmap area owns new, constructors, inheritance and interfaces?
cards.extra: This area is where the language stops being syntax: classes, constructors, fields, inheritance, interfaces, encapsulation, records, packages and access control all live here.
cards.example: Object o = new Object();   // 02 Object Model owns new and constructors

cards.front: Which roadmap area owns HashSet, HashMap and iterators?
cards.extra: Collections is the standard library's data-structure layer: List, Set, Map, Queue and Deque implementations, plus iterators, generics and Optional.
cards.example: java.util.Set seen = new java.util.HashSet<>();   // 04 Collections

cards.front: Which roadmap area explains why synchronized alone may not make a write visible to another thread?
cards.extra: synchronized gives mutual exclusion, but visibility between threads also needs a happens-before edge. Writing through volatile or the same lock creates that edge, and the Java Memory Model defines it.
cards.example:
class Flag {
    volatile boolean ready;   // without volatile another thread may never see the write
}

cards.front: Which roadmap area owns Maven, Gradle and Spring Boot?
cards.extra: Build tools compile, test and package; frameworks supply the runtime structure (dependency-injection container, HTTP layer). Spring Boot is the recommended default, with Quarkus, Play and Javalin as alternatives — Bazel is the exotic third build tool.
cards.example:
plugins { id 'org.springframework.boot' version '3.3.0' }  // 09 Build and Frameworks
java { toolchain { languageVersion = JavaLanguageVersion.of(21) } }

cards.front: Which logging facade do Logback, Log4j2 and TinyLog all plug into?
cards.extra: Your code calls the SLF4J API; a binding (Logback, Log4j2, TinyLog) does the actual logging at runtime. Swapping implementations then needs no source change, which is why the roadmap shows them as siblings.
cards.example:
Logger log = LoggerFactory.getLogger(App.class);  // one API
log.info("started");                              // backend chosen at runtime

cards.front: Which Spring API replaced hand-written JDBC boilerplate?
cards.back: Spring Data JPA (on top of JPA / Hibernate)
cards.extra: Instead of Connection/Statement/ResultSet by hand, you declare a repository interface and Spring generates the implementation, with JPA/Hibernate mapping objects to tables. JDBC still runs underneath.
cards.example: interface UserRepo extends JpaRepository { }   // no SQL, no boilerplate

cards.front: Which JDK 21 feature runs blocking code on very many lightweight threads?
cards.extra: A virtual thread is scheduled by the JVM onto a small pool of carrier threads. Blocking it is cheap, so thread-per-request code scales to hundreds of thousands of tasks without reactive plumbing.
cards.example: Thread.startVirtualThread(() -> System.out.println("light"));

cards.front: Which framework does the roadmap recommend for Java web applications?
cards.extra: Spring Boot packages the Spring ecosystem with auto-configuration and an embedded server, which is why the roadmap marks it recommended. Quarkus targets fast startup and native images; Play and Javalin are lighter.
cards.example:
@SpringBootApplication
class App { public static void main(String[] a) { SpringApplication.run(App.class, a); } }

cards.front: Where does the Java roadmap send you for the backend topics it deliberately skips?
cards.extra: The Java roadmap leaves generic backend topics — HTTP semantics, database design, authentication — to the Backend roadmap so it can stay Java-specific.
cards.example: // HTTP, databases and messaging live in the Backend roadmap, not here

cards.front:
What does this print?

Person a = new Person("Ana");
Person b = a;
b.name = "Bea";
System.out.println(a.name);
cards.extra: b is not a copy: both variables hold the same reference, so writing through b changes the one Person that a points at.
cards.example:
class Person { String name = "Ana"; }
class Demo {
    public static void main(String[] a) {
        Person x = new Person();
        Person y = x;          // same object, not a copy
        y.name = "Bea";
        System.out.println(x.name);   // Bea
    }
}
